answer: An agent economy can require each identity to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it can vote on reputation or claim rewards. A community sets a minimum stake and delays withdrawals; identities caught coordinating fraud lose their bond, while honest agents recover it after the review period. Splitting one agent into many accounts then requires funding every account and risks losing each bond, so a sybil attack becomes costly rather than free. A pigment-marked terrace map viewed through a prism may help explain the design, but the deterrent is the forfeitable stake, not the labels.
